input.question: Why fish can pull oxygen from the water yet not from the air.
input.ground_truth: Fish pull oxygen out of the water using a body part called a *gill*. They have gills on either side of their heads (kind of where our ears are). Gills are made of lots and lots of little thin fins. That way they have lots and lots of surface that touches the water passing by, so there are lots of opportunities for some oxygen passing by to dissolve into them. If you've ever seen someone with long hair underwater, you've seen how their hair kind of floats all around their heads, right? What happens when they come out of the pool? Their hair falls flat onto their heads and kind of all sticks together because it's wet. That's exactly what happens to a fish's gills when you take a fish out of the water. All those little paper-thin fins collapse together and stick together because they're wet and have no water to float in. There isn't enough area left on the surface for them to get the oxygen they need, so they suffocate.

Question: Why fish can pull oxygen from the water yet not from the air.

Answer:

response.prediction: Fish have special organs called gills that help them extract oxygen from water. Gills are made up of thin layers with lots of tiny blood vessels. As water passes over the gills, oxygen from the water moves into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves out. Fish are not able to get oxygen from the air because their bodies are not designed to breathe air like lungs. Their gills can only work in water, where there is enough oxygen dissolved for them to survive. That’s why fish can pull oxygen from water but not from air.
